title: The fenced mandarin tree
translation: Late in autumn I passed through Kurusuno, looking for a village up in the mountains. At the end of a long, mossy path there was a little hermitage, completely alone. The only sound was water dripping from a bamboo pipe buried under leaves. Someone had put chrysanthemums and red leaves on the little altar shelf, so somebody did live there. You really can live like this, I thought, and it moved me.
Then I saw, across the garden, a big mandarin tree, its branches bent with fruit, and a sturdy fence all the way around it. That spoiled it a bit. If only that tree weren't there.

{木|こ}の{葉|は}にうづもるる{筧|かけひ}の{雫|しづく}ならでは、つゆおとなふものなし。
{閼伽棚|あかだな}に、{菊|きく}{紅葉|もみぢ}など{折|を}りちらしたる、さすがに{住|す}む{人|ひと}のあればなるべし。
かくても{在|あ}られけるよと、あはれに{見|み}る{程|ほど}に、かなたの{庭|には}に、{大|おほ}きなる{柑子|かうじ}の{木|き}の、{枝|えだ}もたわわになりたるが、まはりを{厳|きび}しく{囲|かこ}ひたりしこそ、{少|すこ}しことさめて、この{木|き}なからましかばと{覚|おぼ}えしか。
literal: Around the tenth month, I passed a place called Kurusuno and went searching into a certain mountain village; making my way along a long, narrow, mossy path, there was a hermitage, lived in in a lonely way.
Except for the drops of a water pipe buried in tree leaves, nothing at all made a sound.
On the offering shelf, chrysanthemums, autumn leaves and so on were broken off and scattered: it must be because, after all, someone lives there.

As I looked on, moved, thinking 'so one can live even like this', over in the garden a large mandarin tree, its branches bending with fruit, had been strictly fenced all around: that made the feeling fade a little, and I thought, 'if only this tree were not here'.

notes.text: The tenth month of the old lunar calendar, roughly November. Autumn is ending: chrysanthemums and red leaves fit the season.
し is the past auxiliary き, used for things the writer saw himself. So Kenkō tells this as his own experience. (Compare けり in sections 52 and 53, for stories he heard.)

notes.quote: つゆおとなふものなし
notes.text: つゆ … なし: 'not at all'. But つゆ also means 'dew', right after the dripping water pipe. The 1925 edition points out the play on words: the drops and the 'not a drop of sound' meet in one word.
A shelf for offerings of water (閼伽, from Sanskrit argha) to the Buddha. So the hermit is a Buddhist recluse, someone who has given up the world.

notes.quote: まはりを厳しく囲ひたりし
notes.text: The twist of the section. The hermit has given up the world, but not his mandarins: he fenced the tree so that nobody steals the fruit. That is exactly the attachment a recluse should not have, and one fence ruins the whole poetic scene.

notes.quote: こそ、少しことさめて、この木なからましかばと覚えしか
notes.text: こそ … しか: here the realis form is しか, from the past auxiliary き. ことさむ: 'the fun or the mood cools down'.

notes.quote: この木なからましかば
notes.text: ましかば: 'if (it) were…', a wish against the facts. なから + ましかば: 'if only this tree were not there'. Normally the sentence goes on with '…it would be nice' (…まし), but Kenkō leaves that part out.
